title: Genesis, again
tomorrow: before a single commandment, God says something. what?

lines: A NAME CALLED FROM THE KITCHEN.
cards: Someone calls your name from the kitchen, and from the tone alone you know whether you're in trouble or about to be fed. Genesis has a call like that.

Adam and Eve have eaten the fruit, sewn fig leaves together, and hidden among the trees. Then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And the Lord God called Adam, and said to him: Where art thou?" Three words in English.
God isn't lost. So why ask?

teach.h: A JUDGE: COME OUT AND OWN IT.
teach.b: Readers have heard that question two ways, and both have a case. Some hear a judge. The question is a summons: come out and own it.
Listen to Adam's answer. He says he was afraid because he was naked, so he hid. Then, pressed, he points at the woman, and she points at the serpent.
Hiding, then blame. On this reading, God asks so that Adam can tell the truth himself, and he doesn't. Others hear a parent walking through the house, calling.
God goes looking before anyone goes looking for God.
And look what God does before they leave the garden: makes them garments of skins and clothes them. Their fig leaves were their own cover; the skins are God's. Both readings agree on one thing.
The question waits for an answer, and the Bible keeps asking it.
Later, God calls a name, and the reply finally comes, from Abraham: "Here I am." Moses answers the same at the burning bush. The boy Samuel, called in the night, answers it too.

Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Latin Bible, Abraham's answer is one word, adsum, present. Catholic seminarians still answer with it when they're called forward to be ordained. Genesis is still asking.
Here I am is still the answer.

how: Catholics hear Genesis 3 read at Mass and in the Church's prayer; at ordination, each candidate is called by name and answers "present" (in Latin, adsum).

games.q: the garden and the answer — tap the pairs.
p: the cover God made for them

s: God asks 'where art thou?' because Adam can't be found
God isn't lost; readers hear a summons, a search, or both.
'here I am' is Abraham's answer when God calls his name
Genesis 22:1 in the Douay-Rheims; Moses and Samuel answer the same.
after the fruit, God leaves Adam and Eve to cover themselves
God makes them garments of skins and clothes them.

games.q: your study group splits: one side hears God's 'where art thou?' as a judge, your side hears a parent searching. what's the judge side's best case?
o: Adam answers with hiding and blame, so the question calls him to own it.
God truly didn't know where Adam was and needed him to say.
the story shows God likes catching people out in their mistakes.
games.why: the judge reading rests on Adam's reply: afraid, hidden, then blaming. both readings agree the question waits for 'here I am'.

practice: Say your own name quietly, the way someone who loves you would call it from another room. Then answer out loud with Abraham's words: here I am. Say it once more, slower, and let the sit be the room you answered from.

wordCard.voice: Genesis. The book of beginnings, where God first asks where art thou, and someone, later, answers.

orig.note: Latin, Genesis 22:1 in the Vulgate: here I am, present. still answered at ordinations.

carryVoice: Your line: here I am. No fig leaves and no blame, just present and honest. Talk tomorrow.
